title: What is a 1099-DIV form? Reporting dividend income
summary: What is a 1099-DIV form? Learn how dividend income is reported, who receives one, and how investors handle it at tax time. Read on.
body_markdown:
A 1099-DIV form is an important tax document that reports dividend income and certain distributions you received from investments during the tax year. If you own stocks, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), or other dividend-paying investments, you may receive this form from your bank, brokerage firm, or investment company. The institution also sends a copy to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to report the income paid to you.


Understanding what a 1099-DIV form is can help you report your investment earnings accurately and avoid common tax filing mistakes. The form provides a breakdown of different types of income, including ordinary dividends, qualified dividends, capital gain distributions, and other taxable distributions. This distinction matters because ordinary and qualified dividends may be subject to different federal tax rates.


Whether you are filing taxes for the first time or managing an established investment portfolio, knowing how to read your 1099-DIV form is essential. In this guide, we explain what the form covers, who receives it, how to report dividend income, and what to do if you receive one.


## **What is a 1099-DIV form?**


A 1099-DIV form is an IRS tax document used to report dividends and other investment distributions paid to individuals during a tax year. If you own stocks, mutual funds, real estate investment trusts (REITs), or other dividend-paying investments, you may receive this form from the financial institution managing your investments.


The form provides a breakdown of the income you earned, helping you understand what needs to be reported on your federal income tax return. It is one of several documents used to track earnings,[much like the 1099 form](http://grey.co/blog/what-is-a-1099) , which reports different types of income.


#### **Who issues a 1099-DIV Form?**


Banks, brokerage firms, corporations, mutual funds, and other financial institutions issue a 1099-DIV form to investors who receive reportable dividends or distributions. They also send a copy to the IRS so the reported income can be matched with your tax return.


#### **What distributions does it cover?**


The form covers several types of investment income, including:


- **Ordinary dividends:** Regular payments from stocks and mutual funds.
- **Qualified dividends:** Dividends that may qualify for lower federal tax rates.
- **Capital gain distributions:** Profits passed on to investors by mutual funds and REITs.
- **Nondividend distributions:** Payments generally treated as a return of capital rather than taxable income.


## **What does a 1099-DIV report?**


A 1099-DIV form breaks down the different types of dividend income and distributions you receive from investments. Not all these payments are treated the same way for tax purposes, which is why the form separates them into specific categories.


### **Ordinary and qualified dividends**


Ordinary dividends are payments you receive from investments such as stocks and mutual funds. They are reported in Box 1a and are generally taxed as ordinary income.


Qualified dividends are a portion of ordinary dividends that meet certain IRS requirements. They appear separately in Box 1b and may qualify for lower tax rates. The difference matters because the type of dividend you receive can affect how much tax you owe.


Not every dividend automatically qualifies for the lower rate. Factors such as the type of investment and how long you held the shares can determine whether the dividend meets the IRS requirements. This is why the distinction is worth paying attention to when reviewing your tax statement.


### **Capital gain distributions**


A 1099-DIV form also reports capital gain distributions, usually in Box 2a. These are profits that mutual funds and other investment funds pass on to shareholders after selling investments at a gain. They are generally treated as long-term capital gains for tax purposes.


You may receive these distributions even if you did not sell any shares yourself. The fund may have sold investments within its portfolio and passed the resulting gains on to shareholders.


Understanding these categories makes it easier to see how your investments generate income and how that income is reported. It also connects to the bigger picture of[saving vs investing](http://grey.co/blog/saving-vs-investing-short-term-goals) , particularly when considering how different financial choices affect your money over time.


## **Dividends, foreign income, and holding USD**


Receiving dividends from investments outside your home country can mean dealing with more than just the income itself. You may also need to consider the currency in which the money is paid, whether to convert it immediately, and how to hold it in a way that suits your financial needs.


For instance, if your dividends are paid in US dollars, keeping them in a USD account allows you to hold the funds in their original currency without converting them right away. This can be useful if you have future expenses in dollars or simply prefer to decide when to exchange your money.


With[Grey's USD account](http://grey.co/foreign-accounts) , you can receive and hold USD, making it easier to manage dollar-denominated funds. And if you regularly receive money in different currencies, Grey also lets you[hold and convert multiple currencies](http://grey.co/convert) , all from one place.


The two features serve different but connected purposes: one gives you a place to keep your dollar funds, while the other makes managing money across currencies more convenient.


Currency management can also become important when you receive income from different sources. You might earn in one currency, receive dividends in another, and have everyday expenses in a third. Keeping track of these differences helps you understand how much money you actually have available without confusing the original amount with its converted value.


Exchange rates can change over time, so converting money immediately or holding it in its original currency are two separate considerations. Neither option is automatically better; it depends on your expenses, plans, and currency needs.


Whether you choose to hold your dividends in USD or convert them into another currency depends on your financial needs and preferences. Understanding your options can make managing foreign investment income a little less complicated.


## **Who gets a 1099-DIV?**


If you own stocks, mutual funds, or other investments that pay dividends, you may receive a 1099-DIV form at the end of the tax year. Generally, financial institutions and other payers must issue the form when you receive $10 or more in dividends or other reportable distributions during the year.


This threshold applies to ordinary dividends, capital gain distributions, and certain other stock distributions. However, the $10 minimum is not the only reason you might receive the form. If the payer withheld any federal income tax under backup withholding rules or paid foreign taxes on your dividends, it must issue a 1099-DIV regardless of the amount.


There is also a separate threshold for liquidation distributions, which is generally $2,000 under the 2026 reporting rules.


You do not have to meet a minimum investment balance to receive this form. What matters is the income or distributions your investments generate.


One important detail: not receiving a 1099-DIV does not automatically mean your dividend income is exempt from reporting. Taxpayers may still need to report taxable dividend income even when it falls below the reporting threshold.


## Frequently asked questions about the 1099-DIV Form


### **What is a 1099-DIV used for?**


A 1099-DIV is used to report dividends and certain investment distributions you received during the tax year. It helps you and the IRS track investment income that may need to be included on your federal tax return. The form also separates different types of distributions, making it easier to understand their tax treatment.


### **What is the difference between ordinary and qualified dividends?**


Ordinary dividends are generally taxed at your regular income tax rate. Qualified dividends are a portion of ordinary dividends that meet specific IRS requirements and may qualify for lower capital gains tax rates. The difference matters because the type of dividend you receive can affect how much federal tax you owe.


### **Who sends a 1099-DIV?**


Banks, brokerage firms, mutual funds, corporations, and other financial institutions that pay reportable dividends or distributions send a 1099-DIV. They provide a copy to the investor and submit another to the IRS. The form helps both parties keep track of investment income for the relevant tax year.


### **Is dividend income taxable?**


Yes, dividend income is generally taxable in the United States. However, the tax rate depends on the type of dividend, your income, and other applicable tax rules. Ordinary dividends are generally taxed as ordinary income, while qualified dividends may receive lower tax rates if they meet IRS requirements.


### **What about dividends from foreign investments?**


Dividends from foreign investments may also be taxable in the United States, depending on your tax residency and circumstances. They may involve foreign withholding taxes, which can sometimes qualify for a foreign tax credit. Your 1099-DIV may report foreign tax paid, helping you understand what to include when filing your return.


### Can I keep my dividends in US dollars without converting them?


Yes, if your investment provider allows USD withdrawals and you have access to an eligible USD account, you can keep your dividend payments in dollars rather than converting them immediately. This gives you flexibility over when to exchange the funds, depending on your expenses and currency needs.


### Do exchange rates affect foreign dividend income?


Yes. Exchange rates can affect how much your foreign dividend income is worth when converted into your local currency. Even when the original dividend amount stays the same in USD, its equivalent value may change as exchange rates move. This is worth considering when tracking investment income across different currencies.
